body.head: Theatrical Examiner
body.p: The general business of a critic, in seating himself in the Theatre, is to strengthen himself against the three approaching hours; to indulge in the remembrance of what has been, and in the pictures of what ought to be, in an English theatre; and to snatch, as far as the slamming of doors and the fluttering of loungers will suffer him, the occasional relief of the music between the acts, which, compared with the pieces it divides, is like stripes of gold-lace upon a threadbare drugget. To go to the theatre with these anticipations, and be presented with a piece at once new and tolerable, is about as agreeable and surprising as it would be to a London pedestrian to see claret gushing from Piccadilly pump or a laurel-tree starting up in Saint Giles’s. It is therefore not only with pleasure, but with some emotions of gratitude, that the Examiner has to notice a new comedy called Lost and Found, which was produced here on Wednesday, and notwithstanding many defects of the usual kind, is decidedly better than the general run of its fellow dramas. The main story consists of the distresses of a young Officer (Mr. Holland) and a supposed orphan Lady (Mrs. Edwin) whom he loves and maintains, though with perfectly good intentions. Her dependent and solitary situation exposes her, of course, to suspicion and insult, but the inquiries respecting her and her lover, particularly on the part of an old Gentleman (Mr. Wroughton) whom the latter has rescued from ruffians in the street, gradually procure them friends, and at length dissipate the cloud under which they are mysteriously struggling: the grateful stranger, who has just arrived from the East Indies, not only turns out to be his deliverer’s guardian, but finds in the person of the young Lady an only daughter, long supposed to be dead. During his absence abroad, his confidence had been abused by the person (Mr. Lovegrove) to whom he entrusted the young man’s property, as it had also been, long before, by a knavish Attorney, with regard to the existence of his child. The other characters are a rustic servant (Mr. Oxberry), overflowing with manliness and tender attachment, like Mr. Colman's Zekiel Homespun,— a Sir Testy for Mr. Dowton,—Sir Testy’s daughter (Miss Duncan) who coquets,—a Fop (Mr. Russell) who charms her at first but is very pleasantly discarded in the end,—and the Usurer’s Son (Mr. Wrench) who conquers her heart first by outshining the coxcomb in his own way, and afterwards by presenting a manly contrast to his impertinence. These characters and adventures have little pretensions to novelty, as the author seems to acknowledge in the Prologue in speaking of the Attorney; neither do the sentiments or pleasantries in general strike with originality, but the thoughts exhibit a better pith and selection than usual, and some of the sentences are wrought up with a spirit both of sentiment and composition that seems far above the reach of our customary dramatists.—It was, altogether, very well performed. Mr. Oxberry, in the rustic, displayed a mingled feeling and humour, for which the town have hitherto not given him credit, but still much inferior to the consummate skill and apprehension of Emery. Mr. Wrench is pleasant in the gayer part of his character, as he generally is when he has something quick or cunning to say; but he cannot manage the least thing serious or quiet; he is a top, which holds up only by being in a whirl.—Who the author of this piece is, I cannot learn; it appears to me to be in the best style of Mr. Morton, or in not the best style of Miss Chambers; but if it belongs to Mr. Cherry, Mr. Eyre, or Mr. Reynolds, the happy man is very welcome to congratulate himself on my ignorance in not discovering him.
